task: Plan horizon 4 of the agent-agnostic-browser-bridge project — a VERIFICATION-ONLY horizon that records empirical evidence in a real Chrome session (MAIN-world eval vs page CSP; clickAt/hover vs real framework handlers), measures result sizes against real target clients, and ships one hand-verified MCP config snippet in the README — with the 16 page-action surface untouched and all deferred feature work unimplemented.

analysis.objective: Close the project's remaining verification success criteria by gathering—in a real Chrome session and against real target clients—empirical evidence for the deferred CDP-vs-DOM event-fidelity and result-size-cap decisions, and hand-verifying a single documented MCP config snippet, with the 16 page-action surface untouched and all deferred feature work unimplemented.
analysis.successDefinition: Done means: (1) a real-Chrome manual check against at least one real non-trivial site per claim records in discoveries.md/blockers.md whether MAIN-world (0, eval)(code) survives strict page CSPs and whether clickAt/hover produced observable framework-handler effects (a page-side state change, not just the dispatched count), as evidence for the CDP-vs-DOM decision; (2) concrete byte measurements exist for captureTab image blocks and readConsoleMessages/readNetworkRequests results at realistic sizes, exercised through at least two of the available target clients (Claude Code, Gemini CLI; Codex/Cursor only if reachable), plus a measured integer threshold at which an executeScript { value } errors as over-large, all recorded as findings/recommendations only; (3) the README ships one MCP config snippet (command + args) with per-client notes that hand-verification shows works unchanged in at least Claude Code and Gemini CLI; (4) npm run verify passes clean, PAGE_ACTIONS and the MCP tool catalog keep exactly their 16 actions, no new page-action or feature code is added, and decisions.md/blockers.md still record CDP-vs-DOM, result-size cap location/threshold, and tabId as OPEN decisions (a measurement may imply a recommendation, never an implemented decision).
assumptions: Claude Code and Gemini CLI are the two hand-verifiable clients on this machine per horizon-2 discovery; Codex CLI and Cursor are not on PATH, so their coverage is per-client documentation, not live verification.
The horizon-3 roadmap/status files record the outcome of prior real-Chrome checks and the current build/relay/MCP state; horizon 4 re-runs its own check rather than re-deriving prior findings.

npm run verify in tools/chrome-bridge (tsc --noEmit, eslint --max-warnings 0, vitest unit+int) is the real gate for package code; the repo-root PostToolUse lint hook false-positives on tools/chrome-bridge files and is ignored.

The existing shipped caps (MAX_EXECUTE_SCRIPT_RESULT_CHARS=1000000, DEFAULT_MAX_CHARS=200000, entry/text/body caps from capture.ts, read limit clamped to 500) remain shipped behavior; measurements suggesting a different cap location/threshold become recommendations, not code changes.
Existing client-config observations are given external state that the README snippet and per-client docs must accommodate, not modify.
A reachable real site that actually enforces a strict eval-blocking CSP, and a real framework-heavy page with observable click/hover effects, exist and can be loaded in the machine's Chrome.
risks: A real strict-CSP site may reject the injected script for a different reason than the page CSP (host_permissions, Trusted Types, script-injection paths), making the eval evidence site-specific; the check must record the exact site, CSP header, and outcome so the CDP-vs-DOM evidence stays honest.

Whether a real framework handler fired is not directly readable from the dispatched-count result; without an observable page-side effect the check could silently record 'dispatched' as 'handler fired' — the observation method must be explicit.

Gemini CLI registration via a pasted settings.json mcpServers block was recorded open at horizon 2 and never resolved; hand-verification with Gemini CLI may fail, undercutting acceptance criterion 3 — the failure and the actually-working path must be recorded rather than papered over.

Scope creep: measuring 'where the cap lives' or 'what integer is over-large' tempts implementing a cap, tabId, or CDP plumbing — explicitly prohibited by criteria 4-5; this horizon may only produce evidence and recommendations.
Only two clients are hand-verifiable here; reporting the snippet as verified for all four overclaims — Codex and Cursor coverage is documentation-only this horizon.
A heavy read* call or large captureTab during measurement can truncate or hang a client session; bounded probes are needed so 'truncation observed' is recorded as evidence, not a crashed session.
outOfScope: tabId-targeting refactor — user scoped it out; this horizon only produces evidence about the tabId model, never plumbing.
CDP / chrome.debugger / computer-parity family — gated on the CDP-vs-DOM evidence this horizon collects and must stay unimplemented.

Implementing any result-size cap location or threshold — measurement may recommend, may never change shipped limits.
Fixing client config files — external observed state; only the README snippet plus per-client notes ship.
Adding any 17th page action or altering PAGE_ACTIONS / TOOL_CATALOG shape — criterion 4 pins the 16-action surface as unchanged.
Repairing the repo-root PostToolUse lint hook — a known false-positive to ignore, not a defect this horizon fixes.

discoveryFindings.finding: PAGE_ACTIONS has exactly 16 entries: ping, navigateTo, getPageText, readPage, findElement, clickElement, typeText, captureTab, readConsoleMessages, readNetworkRequests, executeScript, navigateBack, navigateForward, reloadTab, clickAt, hover. All consumers are typed Record<PageAction, ...>, and listTools() derives from PAGE_ACTIONS, so the 16-action surface is tsc-pinned.
discoveryFindings.implication: The 16-action pin is compile-time enforced; a PAGE_ACTIONS.length/listTools().length assertion suffices as evidence criterion (4) holds — no new runtime checks needed.

discoveryFindings.finding: src/protocol/types.ts contains NO size-limit constants itself. Limits live in page-actions.ts (DEFAULT_MAX_CHARS=200_000; MAX_EXECUTE_SCRIPT_RESULT_CHARS=1_000_000), capture.ts (MAX_CONSOLE_TEXT_BYTES=8192; MAX_BODY_PREVIEW_BYTES=4096), capture-buffer.ts (DEFAULT_MAX_ENTRIES=500; DEFAULT_READ_LIMIT=100; MAX_READ_LIMIT=500).
discoveryFindings.implication: The 'where does the size cap live' measurement must distinguish extension-side per-action caps from the complete absence of an MCP-layer cap — the MCP layer is the only unguarded place.

discoveryFindings.finding: executeScript handler (page-actions.ts:404-459) validates a non-empty 'code', injects via ports.executeScript(tab.id, fn, [code], { world: 'MAIN' }); the injected fn runs `(0, eval)(code)` (indirect eval, line 416) which is subject to the page's CSP unsafe-eval restriction; a blocked eval throws, is caught, and coerceExecuteScriptOutcome maps it to 'executeScript returned no result — the page may block eval via its Content-Security-Policy'.
discoveryFindings.implication: The real-Chrome CSP check is reproducible: navigate a strict-CSP site, call executeScript with { code }, record whether the reply is { value } or the eval/CSP sentinel. chrome.scripting injection is NOT blocked by page CSP — only the inner eval is, so evidence must record the site's CSP header.

discoveryFindings.finding: NO size guard on the incoming code string; the result-size guard exists twice: inside the injected MAIN-world fn (JSON.stringify(value) compared against MAX_EXECUTE_SCRIPT_RESULT_CHARS=1_000_000, returns ok:false) and extension-side (coerceExecuteScriptOutcome re-checks json.length > 1_000_000 → 'result is too large'). The over-large boundary is exactly a JSON length of 1_000_001 chars.
discoveryFindings.implication: The 'find the integer at which { value } becomes over-large' is defined by a shipped constant — the check confirms the boundary via binary search around 1,000,000 and records it as confirmation, not a new threshold.

discoveryFindings.finding: clickAt (page-actions.ts:461-494) validates x/y, injects a closure doing document.elementFromPoint(px,py), dispatches pointerdown/pointerup/click returning {found,dispatched}; hover (496-527) dispatches pointerover/mouseover = dispatched:2. There is NO mechanism that observes framework-handler effects — no page-side state read, no listener dispatch count, no isTrusted distinction.
discoveryFindings.implication: The event-fidelity check cannot use the tool's own result to prove a handler fired; it must pair clickAt/hover with a follow-up executeScript/getPageText probe reading a page-side state change. Bake the follow-up probe into the check.

discoveryFindings.finding: The MCP layer renders clickAt/hover via the generic text path JSON.stringify(result, null, 2) — { found, dispatched }. ClickAtResult/HoverResult document that synthetic events are untrusted and non-zero dispatched does not guarantee a framework handler reacted.
discoveryFindings.implication: The write-up must interleave the gesture call and the probe call explicitly; the framework-effect evidence comes from the separate probe, not the gesture echo.

discoveryFindings.finding: Grounded extension-side caps: DEFAULT_MAX_CHARS=200_000; MAX_EXECUTE_SCRIPT_RESULT_CHARS=1_000_000; DEFAULT_MAX_ENTRIES=500; DEFAULT_READ_LIMIT=100/MAX_READ_LIMIT=500; MAX_CONSOLE_TEXT_BYTES=8192; MAX_BODY_PREVIEW_BYTES=4096; OUTBOX_LIMIT=100; WORK_SLICE=MAX_CONSOLE_TEXT_BYTES*4+64. captureTab is explicitly UNCAPPED at the extension (data:image/png;base64).

discoveryFindings.implication: No generic MCP-layer cap exists to find; the cap-location decision is strictly extension-side per-action caps (exist) vs a hypothetical new MCP-layer cap (does not). Measurement must observe where clients themselves truncate.

phases.name: Verify eval and synthetic clicks on real pages
phases.goal: Run a hand-driven real-Chrome manual check that exercises the extension's page actions against live external sites and records empirical evidence into the project evidence files. Two claims must be settled: (1) does the executeScript page action's MAIN-world indirect eval `(0, eval)(code)` survive on a real page whose Content-Security-Policy (CSP) header forbids eval (`script-src` without `unsafe-eval`), or does the eval throw and return the 'page may block eval' error sentinel; (2) do the clickAt and hover page actions' synthetic pointer/mouse events actually fire real React/Vue framework handlers on a framework-heavy site — proven only by a follow-up executeScript/getPageText probe reading a page-side state change (open menu, visible tooltip), never by the tool's own {found,dispatched} count. Every outcome is recorded with the site URL, the exact CSP header, and the probe evidence.
phases.rationale: Two earlier checkpoints (horizon 3) closed without empirical proof: nobody has recorded whether MAIN-world eval survives a real strict-CSP page, or whether the synthetic events dispatched by clickAt/hover trigger real SPA handlers that many frameworks ignore because the events are untrusted. These two facts are the evidence the deferred CDP-vs-DOM decision needs before any computer-parity feature can be built, so this phase gathers them in a real Chrome session and records them as findings only — no code changes.
changes: Start the documented ceremony from the README manual check: run `npm run relay`, run `npm run build:extension`, load `tools/chrome-bridge/dist/extension` unpacked in chrome://extensions, and connect an MCP client that uses the chrome-bridge stdio entry.

Navigate to one real site that sends a strict Content-Security-Policy header (script-src without 'unsafe-eval'); call the executeScript page action with {code: "document.title"} and record in discoveries.md the site URL, the exact CSP header, and whether the reply was a {value} result or the 'page may block eval' error sentinel.

Navigate to a real React/Vue SPA with observable tooltip or menu state; call clickAt at the trigger element's x/y and hover at the same point, then immediately run a follow-up executeScript or getPageText probe that reads a page-side state change (open class, tooltip visibility, counter) — the gesture's own {found,dispatched} output alone must not count as proof a handler fired.

Append the per-site evidence records to discoveries.md and annotate the two still-open horizon-3 blocker entries (CSP-eval and synthetic clickAt/hover) with the recorded outcomes; keep the CDP-vs-DOM decision recorded OPEN in decisions.md, recording only evidence and never flipping the decision.
Run `npm run verify` in tools/chrome-bridge to confirm the evidence-gathering session introduced no code that breaks typecheck, lint, or the unit tests.

phases.expectedResult: One evidence record set in the project memory files: for the strict-CSP site a record of site URL, exact CSP header, and executeScript outcome (value versus eval sentinel); for the SPA site a record of each clickAt/hover gesture paired with its follow-up probe showing whether a framework handler visibly reacted — with the two horizon-3 blocker entries annotated by those outcomes and the CDP-vs-DOM decision still OPEN.

rubric.label: Real strict-CSP site evidence for MAIN-world eval
rubric.ruleStatement: The deliverable must prove what executeScript's MAIN-world indirect eval `(0, eval)(code)` does on a real site whose CSP actually forbids eval, in a form that can be re-run from the record alone. Scale: 10 means the outcome is confirmed on two unrelated strict-CSP sites with the raw header copied verbatim and the result text quoted exactly, so no reviewer could ask for more; 8 is the expected score for a competent, complete record (one real strict-CSP site with URL, exact header, and verbatim outcome); minScore 7 is the bar for ACCEPTABLE evidence for at least one real non-trivial site per the caller's criterion, with URL, header, and outcome all present even if header capture used a helper rather than a raw copy.
passCriteria: In discovery.md of the phase record, confirm it names a public URL of a real external site — not a localhost page, a data: URL, or a page the executor authored.

Confirm the record states the exact Content-Security-Policy header the site sent in its response (or says it could not be read and names the method used), and that the policy forbids eval, i.e. script-src / script-src-elem lacks 'unsafe-eval'.
Confirm the record states the executeScript result verbatim: the returned value on success, or the exact 'page may block eval' sentinel text on failure — not a paraphrase like 'it worked'.
Confirm the site is non-trivial: it runs substantial third-party runtime scripts under its own deployed CSP, so the test exercises a real deployment's policy rather than a controlled fixture.
Confirm the record states which of the two possible outcomes occurred (value versus eval sentinel) in a way a grader cannot confuse.
failureExamples: The site's CSP actually allows 'unsafe-eval' — the record asserts strictness from memory and never quotes the header, so a passed eval measures nothing and the recorded claim is void.
The executor built a local fixture whose CSP header they wrote themselves and recorded it as real-site evidence, capturing their own policy rather than a real deployment's.
The record quotes a parsed or normalized header from a security analyzer instead of the raw response header, so 'exact header' cannot be re-verified against the live site.

rubric.label: Framework-handler proof from a page-side probe
rubric.ruleStatement: The record must show whether clickAt/hover synthetic events actually reached real React/Vue framework handlers, and the only admissible proof is a follow-up executeScript/getPageText probe reading a page-side state change — the tool's own {found,dispatched} count must never be cited as proof. Scale: 10 means every gesture is paired with an unambiguous, timing-controlled, reproducible probe, so no reviewer could ask for more; 8 is the expected score for a competent, complete record (clickAt and hover each paired with a distinct page-side probe on a real framework-heavy site); minScore 7 is the bar for ACCEPTABLE — at least one gesture type on at least one real non-trivial site, with the gesture output AND a distinct page-side probe present, one gesture even if honestly reported as 'not handled'.
passCriteria: In the phase record, confirm it names a real framework-heavy site (React/Vue/Angular/Svelte) with substantial client-side handlers.
For each recorded gesture, confirm the record gives the target element selector and x/y coordinates plus the gesture's own {found,dispatched} output.

Confirm each clickAt/hover gesture is followed by a probe result that is observably NOT the gesture echo: an executeScript return value or getPageText excerpt containing a page-side state datum (a class/attribute/text change, a menu or tooltip visibility change) that only a framework handler could set.

Confirm the record states, per gesture, whether the probe showed the handler fired or did not fire, and that a 'not handled' conclusion was checked after a framework state-commit delay before being recorded.
Confirm the record nowhere claims proof from {found,dispatched} alone.
failureExamples: The record defends 'the framework handled the click' by quoting {found: true, dispatched: true} with no page-side probe after it — the dispatcher asserting its own dispatch.

The probe ran immediately after dispatch and read a false negative because the framework batches or defers state commits (React 18 auto-batching, async effects), and the record concludes 'handlers ignore synthetic events' without re-reading after a settle delay.

The gesture targeted coordinates over no interactive element (a blank area of the SPA), so a 'not handled' outcome reflects the wrong target rather than untrusted-event policy, and the record never shows which element was aimed at.

rubric.label: Evidence lands in the project memory files
rubric.ruleStatement: Every claim's evidence must be findable in the documented project memory files (discoveries.md records plus appended blocker annotations), not in chat logs, PR bodies, or scratch notes, so the deferred-decision reader can act without re-running the session. Scale: 10 means every fact used downstream is in the two files and cross-referenced, so no reviewer could ask for more; 8 is the expected score for a competent, complete write-up (all session evidence present in discoveries.md and both relevant blockers annotated); minScore 7 is the bar for ACCEPTABLE — every claim's evidence appears in at least one of the two project files, even if cross-referencing is light.
passCriteria: Grep the repo for a unique string from each recorded site URL; each appears inside docs/roadmaps/agent-agnostic-browser-bridge/discoveries.md.
In blockers.md, the horizon-3 entry covering CSP-eval and synthetic clickAt/hover has an appended outcome note citing the corresponding discovery record.
No evidence needed for the CDP-vs-DOM decision exists only outside those two files (PR body, chat transcript, repo-root scratch markdown, /tmp notes).
failureExamples: The session was fully run and the conclusions posted in the PR description, but discoveries.md still contains no external-site record, so the next executor must rebuild the evidence from scratch.
The executor kept the session log in a scratch file at the repo root that is not part of the memory files the decision-maker reads, so graders cannot find the evidence in the documented location.

rubric.label: Deferred decisions remain OPEN, findings are recommendations only
rubric.ruleStatement: The deferred decisions (CDP-vs-DOM event fidelity, result-size cap location/threshold, tabId targeting model) must remain OPEN after this phase: the relevant blockers are annotated with outcomes but not marked RESOLVED, decisions.md statuses do not flip, and any conclusion phrased as a decision must instead be labeled a recommendation, except where a measurement makes a decision obviously forced and is recorded explicitly as a recommendation rather than an implementation. Scale: 10 means decision statuses are provably unchanged and every finding is framed as evidence with its open question restated, so no reviewer could ask for more; 8 is the expected score for a competent, complete session (blockers stay OPEN with annotations, decisions.md statuses untouched, no code implements a decision); minScore 7 is the bar for ACCEPTABLE — blockers.md and decisions.md show no DECIDED/RESOLVED/IMPLEMENTED status change and the git diff implements no deferred decision.
passCriteria: Open blockers.md: the horizon-3 CSP-eval/synthetic-event entry and the result-size-cap entry are still marked OPEN, with their appended outcomes attached as annotations rather than status changes.
Open decisions.md: the CDP-vs-DOM entry and any result-size or tabId-model entry still read as open questions; nothing reads as 'decided' or 'implemented' unless clearly labeled a recommendation.

Git diff against the phase-start commit shows no source change that implements a decision (no eval-mode switch, no result-size cap constant, no new tabId model), and any written recommendation uses the word 'recommendation' and does not claim the decision was made.
If a measurement made a decision 'obvious', confirm the obviousness is recorded under a clearly labeled recommendation with the decision itself still recorded as open.
failureExamples: The successful eval convinces the executor that the CSP-eval blocker is rewritten as RESOLVED and 'we will use MAIN-world indirect eval' is recorded as a made decision — closing, before the horizon said it was allowed to, a decision this phase was only to inform.
A recommendation is phrased in implemented-decision language ('we cap results at 4MB at the MCP layer') even though no code ships it, silently flipping the decision's status for every later reader.

phases.name: Measure result sizes against two clients
phases.goal: Produce byte-size measurements — records plus a recommendation, never code changes — for the 'where does the result-size cap live' deferred decision, exercised through real target-client sessions (Claude Code and Gemini CLI). Measure: (a) the captureTab page action's returned image content block (PNG base64) byte size; (b) the readConsoleMessages and readNetworkRequests capture-buffer-read text-result byte sizes at realistic limits (100 vs 500 entries, approaching the ~4MB worst case implied by the 8192-byte per-entry console cap); (c) the executeScript page action's {value} JSON-length boundary at MAX_EXECUTE_SCRIPT_RESULT_CHARS = 1,000,000 chars, finding the exact integer at which the result errors as over-large. All shipped caps stay unchanged; only discoveries.md/blockers.md receive findings and a recommendation.
phases.rationale: The bridge's MCP layer renders every text result as pretty-printed JSON with no truncation, and captureTab is deliberately uncapped, so large responses can reach megabytes and different target clients handle that very differently. Before anyone decides whether the size cap belongs at the extension, at the MCP layer, or nowhere, this machine needs real measured numbers from live client sessions rather than guesses — the deferred decision stays open, but it now has data.
changes: With the relay, the built extension, and a busy real tab running, call readConsoleMessages and readNetworkRequests first with limit 100 and then limit 500, and record the byte size of each returned text block (the 500-entry case approaches the ~4MB worst case implied by the 8192-byte per-entry console text cap), keeping each probe inside the 30-second controller timeout.
Call captureTab on the same tab and record the byte size of the returned image content block (the raw PNG base64, MIME type image/png), which the extension leaves uncapped.

Call executeScript with expressions whose JSON round-trip lengths sit just below and just above 1,000,000 characters, and record the exact integer at which the 'executeScript result is too large (N chars; limit 1000000)' error starts appearing.

Drive the read* and executeScript probes through at least two real target clients — Claude Code via the repo-root .mcp.json entry and Gemini CLI via `gemini mcp add` — so client-side truncation or rejection is observed where it actually happens and recorded as evidence.

Append every measured byte size plus one recommendation for where the result-size cap should live to discoveries.md, annotate the still-open result-size-cap blocker with the numbers, and keep the decision OPEN in decisions.md.
phases.boundedContext: result-size behavior — MCP result rendering and target clients
inputs: The shipped extension-side caps in src/protocol/capture.ts, src/extension/capture-buffer.ts and src/extension/page-actions.ts (MAX_CONSOLE_TEXT_BYTES=8192, MAX_BODY_PREVIEW_BYTES=4096, DEFAULT_MAX_ENTRIES=500, MAX_READ_LIMIT=500, MAX_EXECUTE_SCRIPT_RESULT_CHARS=1_000_000)

The MCP result-rendering rules in src/mcp/server.ts: captureTab becomes a single image content block, every other action becomes a pretty-printed JSON text block, and no truncation exists anywhere at the MCP layer
Real target-client sessions, hand-verifiable only for Claude Code and Gemini CLI — discovery confirms no codex or cursor binary exists on PATH
discoveries.md and blockers.md as record targets, where the result-size-cap blocker line is still OPEN
phases.expectedResult: One measurement record in discoveries.md: byte sizes for the captureTab image block, for readConsoleMessages/readNetworkRequests at limit 100 and limit 500, and the confirmed 1,000,000/1,000,001-char executeScript {value} boundary, all recorded from at least two real target-client sessions with client-side truncation observed where it occurred — plus a single recorded recommendation for the result-size cap location, the resolve-result-size blocker annotated, and the decision left OPEN.

rubric.label: Concrete byte sizes recorded for every probe
rubric.ruleStatement: The deliverable records each required measurement as an exact integer with a unit and the probe configuration that produced it. 10 means no reviewer could ask for another number; 8 is the expected score for a competent, complete run (all probes present, one probe config implied rather than stated); 7 is the acceptable bar: each of the three probe families (captureTab image block, read* at limit 100 and 500, executeScript boundary) appears with at least one exact number.
passCriteria: The record states a concrete number in bytes for the captureTab image block as the client receives it — the raw PNG base64 payload (mimeType image/png) with the data-URL prefix stripped — as an integer with the unit bytes.

For readConsoleMessages and readNetworkRequests the record contains four sizes: each action at limit 100 and at limit 500, each an integer plus unit, reflecting the pretty-printed JSON text block the MCP layer renders rather than the compact buffer payload.
Every recorded size names the probe configuration that produced it (page action, limit value, tab/page state) so an independent executor can rerun the probe and reproduce the number.
No recorded value is expressed as a range, a tilde approximation, a unit-less integer, or a prose word such as 'large'.
failureExamples: All probes ran against a nearly empty page, so every recorded size is a handful of KB and the multi-megabyte case implied by 8192-byte console entries times 500 entries never appears — each number is technically real but the cap decision has no data from the high end it was meant to inform.

The read* sizes were taken from the extension's compact response object instead of the pretty-printed JSON text block the MCP server actually ships, so every number understates what crosses the client boundary.

rubric.label: Measurements exercised through both target clients
rubric.ruleStatement: The numbers are attributed to the real client session that produced them — Claude Code via the repo-root .mcp.json chrome-bridge entry and Gemini CLI via 'gemini mcp add'. 10 means every size line names its producing client and both clients contributed across the probe suite; 8 is a competent, complete run where both clients are named but one covered only a single probe family; 7 is the acceptable bar: at least one real measurement is attributed to each of the two clients and no recorded size is unattributed.
passCriteria: At least one recorded size is explicitly attributed to Claude Code and at least one is explicitly attributed to Gemini CLI — the client name appears on the size lines themselves, not only in a summary sentence.

The record flags any size that did not come from a real client session (e.g. piped straight into the MCP server via a script), and 'measured in client X' is only claimed where a session produced the number.
For the Gemini CLI measurements the record notes that the server was registered via 'gemini mcp add', since a pasted mcpServers block has never been verified for that client.
failureExamples: Every byte size is attributed to the Claude Code session and the Gemini CLI numbers were filled in by copying — the developer ran one client and assumed client-side behavior is identical, so a truncation that only Gemini performs is absent from the evidence.

The sizes were gathered by a Node script talking to the MCP server directly, and lines reading 'verified in Claude Code and Gemini CLI' are backed by no session — the two-client requirement is met by prose, not by evidence.

rubric.label: executeScript over-large boundary pinned to an exact integer
rubric.ruleStatement: The record pins the exact JSON-length boundary at which executeScript starts erroring. 10 means a succeeding and a failing integer are both recorded a few chars apart with the server's own error text quoted and the client's handling of the failure noted; 8 is the expected score for a competent, complete run: both integers recorded and the error message matched; 7 is the acceptable bar: a failing probe recorded at an explicit integer with the 'too large' error, plus a succeeding probe at an explicit integer just below it.
passCriteria: A succeeding probe is recorded with an explicit result-JSON length in chars (e.g. '1,000,000 chars OK').

A failing probe is recorded with its explicit length (e.g. '1,000,001 chars fails') and the recorded error text matches the shipped message 'executeScript result is too large (N chars; limit 1000000)' with the same N the server reported.

The recorded lengths measure the expression's serialized result value (the JSON round-trip), not the expression source text or a copied constant — the boundary is evidenced by live probes that actually cross it, not extrapolated from MAX_EXECUTE_SCRIPT_RESULT_CHARS.
failureExamples: The boundary was computed by reading MAX_EXECUTE_SCRIPT_RESULT_CHARS and assuming equality — the record shows no probe that ever ran an actually over-large expression, so a boundary is quoted with no failing observation.

The developer measured the length of the input expression string instead of the serialized result value, so the recorded boundary is off by the JSON quoting overhead and a later probe near the recorded number errors or succeeds unexpectedly.

rubric.label: Client-side handling of large results recorded as evidence
rubric.ruleStatement: For every size at the realistic upper end, the record states what the producing client actually did with the result — delivered whole, truncated, or rejected — and treats that as evidence. 10 means every size line carries the client's observed behavior and client-side truncation is captured wherever it happened; 8 is a competent, complete run: behavior recorded per client for the upper-end probes; 7 is the acceptable bar: for every limit-500 read and the captureTab image, the record states the client's behavior or explicitly records that no truncation was observed.
passCriteria: For each client session that produced a limit-500 read or the captureTab image, the record answers: did the client return the block whole, cut it off, or error — and if truncated, which side (client or bridge) did the cutting.
Where a client truncated or rejected a result, that event appears in discoveries.md with the size at which it occurred; where a client delivered the full block, the record says so explicitly.
The cap-location recommendation reflects the observed per-client behavior — it is not written as if all clients behave alike when the record shows they do not.
failureExamples: Gemini CLI truncated the 500-entry read at its own limit, but the developer treated truncation as a botched measurement, shrank the page, and recorded only the small full result — the very evidence the cap-location decision needs silently disappeared.

A probe timed out inside the 30-second controller window or the client dropped the connection, and the developer recorded the extension-side response size as the delivered size — the record claims a client delivery that never happened.

rubric.label: Evidence recorded; decision left OPEN; surface untouched
rubric.ruleStatement: This horizon ships records, not code: changes touch only docs/roadmaps/agent-agnostic-browser-bridge/discoveries.md and blockers.md, the result-size-cap decision stays OPEN in decisions.md, and the 16-action PAGE_ACTIONS surface is unchanged. 10 means the diff contains exactly the two record files, the blocker is annotated with the measured numbers, and nothing else moved; 8 is a competent, complete run with the same and at most an incidental whitespace-only diff; 7 is the acceptable bar: no shipped code or config changed, the decision file still says OPEN, and all 16 page actions are intact.
passCriteria: git diff --stat shows modifications only under docs/roadmaps/agent-agnostic-browser-bridge/ — nothing under tools/chrome-bridge/src, the build configs, or any .json config, so the shipped caps in capture.ts, capture-buffer.ts and page-actions.ts are byte-identical.
PAGE_ACTIONS in tools/chrome-bridge/src/protocol/actions.ts still lists exactly the same 16 entries — no action added, renamed, or removed.

decisions.md still marks the result-size-cap decision OPEN; any new line is phrased as a recommendation, not a decision; and the blockers.md result-size-cap line is annotated with the measured bytes and remains unresolved.
failureExamples: Seeing a 1.2 MB captureTab block, the developer added a hard cap in src/mcp/server.ts 'just to be safe' — the diff now shows a shipped behavioral change that decides the deferred decision implicitly.

The measurements were recorded and the decisions.md result-size-cap line was flipped to 'resolved (recommendation: no cap)' — the status changed from OPEN with no decision process, so the decision state the next horizon inherits is wrong.

phases.healerHint: The most likely failure is that sizes get measured and written up from a single Claude Code session (with Gemini CLI coverage asserted in prose) and from the extension-side responses rather than the rendered MCP blocks the clients actually received — so the fastest fix is, before writing any number, to run each probe once per client and paste each client-visible block size (or the exact truncation/error the client surfaced) next to it.
